components.note: 扌 (hand) — 掩 describes covering or shutting something with the hand.
奄 (yǎn) gives the sound — an exact match with 掩.
扌 (hand) — represents the act of guarding or defending.
户 (door/household) — protecting one's home gave 护 its meaning 'to protect, guard.'

example.hanzi: 队员们互相掩护,安全撤退了。
example.pinyin: Duìyuánmen hùxiāng yǎnhù, ānquán chètuì le.
example.english: The team members covered for each other and retreated safely.
example.fact: 掩护 layers two "hand" actions together — 掩 ("to cover," hand radical 扌 + phonetic 奄) and 护 ("to protect," hand radical 扌 + 户 "door/household") — and the same word covers both a soldier physically shielding a comrade and, by extension, someone covering up another person's wrongdoing, much like English "cover for someone."

components.note: 钅 (metal) — early mirrors were made of polished bronze.
竟 (jìng) is an exact match for the sound of 镜.
A simple drawing of a swaddled baby — arms reaching out, legs bundled together in a wrap.

example.hanzi: 她站在镜子前梳头发。
example.pinyin: Tā zhàn zài jìngzi qián shū tóufa.
example.english: She stood in front of the mirror combing her hair.
example.fact: 镜 pairs the metal radical 钅 with the phonetic 竟 (jìng) — a reminder that before glass mirrors became common, Chinese mirrors were disks of polished bronze, which is why the character for "mirror" is built on "metal" rather than "glass."

components.note: 忄 (heart) — 情 relates to feelings and emotions.
青 (qīng) gives the sound — 情 is pronounced qíng, a close match differing only in tone.
A simple line drawing of a person's legs seen from the side, used to depict a human being.

example.hanzi: 她的情人每天都给她写信。
example.pinyin: Tā de qíngrén měitiān dōu gěi tā xiě xìn.
example.english: Her lover writes to her every day.
example.fact: 情人 pairs 情 ("feeling," built on the heart radical 忄) with 人 ("person"), but unlike the neutral 男朋友/女朋友 ("boyfriend/girlfriend"), it carries a stronger, sometimes illicit romantic charge — closer to English "lover" than to "significant other" — which is also why 情人节 ("Valentine's Day") reaches for this word rather than a plainer one.

components.note: 纟 (silk/thread) — 经 originally referred to the vertical warp threads in weaving.
工 (gōng) gives a related sound cue for 经 (jīng), reflecting an older, closer pronunciation link between the two.
The 曲-shaped top pictures a bundle of bamboo strips, an ancient book.
八 below pictures two hands supporting the book, giving 典 its meaning 'classic text, standard.'

example.hanzi: 这部电影已经成为经典。
example.pinyin: Zhè bù diànyǐng yǐjīng chéngwéi jīngdiǎn.
example.english: This movie has already become a classic.
example.fact: 经 originally referred to the vertical warp threads in weaving before extending to mean "canon, scripture," while 典 pictures a bundle of bamboo strips — an ancient book — held up by two hands. 经典 fuses two separate words for "authoritative text" into one compound meaning "classic."

components.note: 氵 (water) — 活 relates to water flowing, a symbol of life and vitality.
舌 (shé) gives a hint of the sound — 活 is pronounced huó, a connection that has shifted over time.
力 depicts the blade of a plow — since plowing fields took great physical effort, the shape came to represent strength or power.

example.hanzi: 年轻人充满活力。
example.pinyin: Niánqīng rén chōngmǎn huólì.
example.english: Young people are full of energy.
example.fact: 活 (water radical 氵 + phonetic 舌) evokes life as something flowing and unstill, while 力 depicts the blade of a plow, the ancient symbol of physical exertion — together 活力 paints vitality as flowing strength rather than mere existence.

components.note: 图 is the simplified form of 圖, which pictured a district's borders 啚 enclosed within a boundary 囗 — an old image of a map, giving 图 its meaning 'picture, chart, map.'
⺺ — an abstract mark meant to depict strokes made by a writing brush, the origin of 书's meaning 'book, document, letter.'
饣 (food) points to a place where meals are served.
官 pictures an official hall or residence, giving 馆 its sense of a large public building.

example.hanzi: 我每天下午去图书馆看书。
example.pinyin: Wǒ měitiān xiàwǔ qù túshūguǎn kàn shū.
example.english: I go to the library every afternoon to read.
example.fact: 图书馆 is almost perfectly transparent — 图 ("picture/chart") + 书 ("book") + 馆 ("hall") literally spell out "picture-and-book hall" — a modern compound coined to name the Western-style public library, distinct from older native terms like 藏书楼 ("book-storage tower") for a private book collection.

components.note: 日 (sun) — 显 relates to something bright and clearly visible in the light
业 (yè) gives a loose sound connection to 显's reading xiǎn
寸 (a hand) reaching for 旦 (originally 貝, a shell used as currency) — a picture of grasping something valuable, hence 'to obtain, to get.'

example.hanzi: 她今天显得特别开心。
example.pinyin: Tā jīntiān xiǎnde tèbié kāixīn.
example.english: She seems especially happy today.
example.fact: 显得 must be followed by an adjective describing how something comes across (显得 + adj.), the same way English "seems" works — it can't take a noun object directly, so "seems like an expert" needs the extra word 像 (显得像专家), not a bare noun after 显得.

components.note: 匕 (a kneeling person) — a mourner bowed down in grief.
歹 (skeletal remains) — the corpse being mourned, the source of 死's meaning 'to die, dead.'
开-shaped bars picture a cell or restraint.
刂 (knife) adds the idea of physical punishment, giving 刑 its meaning 'punishment, penalty.'

example.hanzi: 那名罪犯被判处死刑。
example.pinyin: Nà míng zuìfàn bèi pànchǔ sǐxíng.
example.english: That criminal was sentenced to the death penalty.
example.fact: 死刑's two characters need no unpacking — 死 ("to die") plus 刑 ("punishment," itself pairing bars 开 with a knife 刂) name the death penalty as literally as English does, sitting at the most severe end of China's ladder of criminal penalties (刑罚).

components.note: 辶 (to walk) — 进 relates to advancing or entering, both movement-related.
井 (jǐng) gives a close sound cue — 进 is pronounced jìn, sharing similar consonant and vowel sounds.
止 (a footprint), shown twice — one foot placed in front of the other, the source of 步's meaning 'step, pace.'

example.hanzi: 你的中文进步很快。
example.pinyin: Nǐ de Zhōngwén jìnbù hěn kuài.
example.english: Your Chinese is progressing very quickly.
example.fact: 进步 works as both a verb ("to improve," 他进步了 "he's improved") and a noun/adjective ("progress; progressive," as in 进步人士 "progressive people") — one word doing the job that English splits across "progress," "improve," and "progressive."

components.note: 辶 (to walk) — 追 relates to moving in pursuit of someone or something
㠯 (yǐ) gives a sound distantly related to 追's reading zhuī, having drifted apart over time

example.hanzi: 他一直在追求自己的音乐梦想。
example.pinyin: Tā yìzhí zài zhuīqiú zìjǐ de yīnyuè mèngxiǎng.
example.english: He has always been pursuing his dream of music.
example.fact: 追求 covers chasing an abstract goal (追求梦想, "to pursue a dream") and romantically courting a person (追求她, "to woo her") with the same verb — Chinese leans on this word for courtship more heavily than English speakers might expect from "pursue" alone.

components.note: 冖 (a roof/house) — the home being welcomed into.
友 (a friend) — brought close into one's home; the traditional form 愛 also includes 心 ('heart') in the middle — the source of 爱's meaning 'to love.'
A stylized drawing of orchid blossoms and leaves growing up from the ground.

example.hanzi: 他的祖父母来自爱尔兰。
example.pinyin: Tā de zǔfùmǔ láizì Ài'ěrlán.
example.english: His grandparents are from Ireland.
example.fact: 爱尔兰 is a sound-only transliteration of "Ireland" — 爱 ("love") and 兰 ("orchid") contribute nothing to the meaning here, but they're conventionally pleasant characters that Chinese reserves for rendering foreign place names it wants to sound agreeable, unlike some more neutral characters used for less favored names historically.

components.note: 禾 (grain, a growing rice or wheat plant) — 利 pictures a harvest.
刂 (knife) — cutting grain at harvest time was a clear benefit or gain, giving 利 its meaning 'profit' or 'advantage.'

example.hanzi: 亨利是我们班唯一的外国学生。
example.pinyin: Hēnglì shì wǒmen bān wéiyī de wàiguó xuésheng.
example.english: Henry is the only foreign student in our class.
example.fact: 亨利 is a pure sound transliteration of "Henry" — 亨 (hēng) independently means "smooth, prosperous" (as in the Book of Changes) but contributes nothing to the name here. The same two characters, written in lowercase as "henry," also happen to name the SI unit of electrical inductance, honoring physicist Joseph Henry.

components.note: 艹 (plant) — 苹 names a fruiting plant.
平 (píng) gives the sound — an exact match with 苹.
田 (here representing round fruit, not its usual meaning 'field') — 果 pictures fruit hanging from branches.
木 (tree) — fruit growing on a tree gave 果 its meaning 'fruit' and, more broadly, 'result.'

example.hanzi: 我每天早上吃一个苹果。
example.pinyin: Wǒ měitiān zǎoshang chī yí gè píngguǒ.
example.english: I eat an apple every morning.
example.fact: 苹 exists mainly to write this one word — it pairs the plant radical 艹 with the phonetic 平 (píng) purely for sound, carrying no independent meaning outside 苹果, a common pattern for characters coined specifically to name a fruit or other borrowed thing.

components.note: Originally a pictograph of a musical bell or instrument hung in a frame; this shape was later reused to write the unrelated directional word 南, 'south.'

example.hanzi: 冬天,他喜欢去南方过冬。
example.pinyin: Dōngtiān, tā xǐhuan qù nánfāng guòdōng.
example.english: In winter, he likes to go south to spend the winter.
example.fact: 南, like the other cardinal-direction characters 东西北, has an ancient pictographic origin unrelated to direction — it's thought to have first depicted a hanging bell or musical instrument, its shape simply borrowed later to write the unrelated word "south."

components.note: 大 (a person, arms outstretched) — represents a human being.
一 (a line, here representing the sky) — drawn above a person, showing what is above them: the heavens, hence 'sky, day.'
屮 (a young shoot) growing up out of 土 (earth/soil) — a picture of new life emerging from the ground.

example.hanzi: 她天生就有一副好嗓子。
example.pinyin: Tā tiānshēng jiù yǒu yí fù hǎo sǎngzi.
example.english: She was born with a wonderful voice.
example.fact: 天生 literally means "born of heaven" (天 "sky/heaven" + 生 "to be born"), reflecting an older worldview that treated innate talent as a gift bestowed from above — much like the English idiom "a natural," which also frames unlearned ability as something given rather than earned.

components.note: 亻 (person) — 傻 describes a state of mind a person is in.
囟 (the top of the head), together with a striking motion below, pictures someone being hit on the head — the odd image behind 傻's meaning 'foolish.'
A simple drawing of a swaddled baby — arms reaching out, legs bundled together in a wrap.

example.hanzi: 别把我当傻子。
example.pinyin: Bié bǎ wǒ dàng shǎzi.
example.english: Don't treat me like a fool.
example.fact: 傻 combines 亻 ("person") with an element depicting a blow to the crown of the head (囟) — a blunt visual joke suggesting someone whose wits have been knocked loose, the likely picture behind its meaning "foolish, stupid."

components.note: 氵 (water) — 浴 relates to washing with water.
谷 (gǔ) gives a sound only distantly related to yù today, having drifted apart over time.
宀 (roof) — 室 refers to an enclosed room under a roof
至 (zhì) gives the sound — an exact match with 室's reading shì

example.hanzi: 浴室里的热水器坏了。
example.pinyin: Yùshì lǐ de rèshuǐqì huài le.
example.english: The water heater in the bathroom is broken.
example.fact: 浴室 names the room by function — 浴 ("to bathe") + 室 ("room") — and in everyday Mainland usage leans toward a dedicated bathing/shower room, while the more common word for a full bathroom including the toilet is 卫生间 ("hygiene room"), a distinction English's single word "bathroom" doesn't force speakers to make.

components.note: 女 (woman) — 婚 relates to marriage, historically centered on the wife.
昏 (hūn) gives the sound — an exact match with 婚.

example.hanzi: 他在海边向她求婚了。
example.pinyin: Tā zài hǎibiān xiàng tā qiúhūn le.
example.english: He proposed to her on the beach.
example.fact: 求婚 usually takes its target with the coverb 向 (向她求婚, "to propose to her") rather than as a bare direct object — learners transferring the English pattern "propose to her" often try 求婚她 by mistake, which sounds off to native ears.

meanings: short stories of the Tang and Song Dynasty

components.note: 亻 (person) — relates to 传's meaning 'to pass on, transmit,' something passed from person to person.
专 (zhuān) gives a sound hint — 传 is pronounced chuán, sharing the same rhyme though the initial consonant differs.
大 (a person, arms outstretched) — represents a rider.
可 here is said to depict a mount — a person riding in an unusual way gave 奇 its meaning 'strange, odd, remarkable.'

example.hanzi: 他的一生充满传奇色彩。
example.pinyin: Tā de yìshēng chōngmǎn chuánqí sècǎi.
example.english: His life was filled with a legendary quality.
example.fact: 传奇 began as the specific name for a genre of marvel tales and dramatic romances from the Tang and Song dynasties before its modern sense of "legendary, larger-than-life" grew out of that literary label — much as English "epic" widened from a specific poetic genre into a casual adjective.

components.note: 人 (people) over 云 (clouds/say) — a picture of people gathering and speaking together, related to 会's meanings 'to meet' and 'to know how to.'
冂 (a simplified eye shape in 见's modern form) — emphasizes the act of seeing.
儿 (a person) — a person with an emphasized eye above gives 见 its meaning 'to see.'

example.hanzi: 两国领导人今天举行了会见。
example.pinyin: Liǎng guó lǐngdǎorén jīntiān jǔxíngle huìjiàn.
example.english: The leaders of the two countries held a meeting today.
example.fact: 会见 sits at the formal, diplomatic end of Chinese's "to meet" vocabulary, reserved for official meetings between officials or dignitaries — everyday meetings with friends instead use 见面 or the bare verb 见, a register distinction English's single verb "to meet" doesn't mark.

components.note: 土 (here representing a person swinging their arms, not its usual meaning 'earth') — depicts someone in motion.
止 (a foot) — combined with the moving figure above, 走 shows a person walking or running.
足 (foot) — relates to 路's meaning 'road, path,' something walked on with feet.
各 (gè) served as the phonetic base; its pronunciation has since drifted well away from lù.

example.hanzi: 医生建议他每天走路半小时。
example.pinyin: Yīshēng jiànyì tā měitiān zǒulù bàn xiǎoshí.
example.english: The doctor recommended he walk for half an hour every day.
example.fact: 走路 specifically emphasizes moving under one's own two feet — its bare root 走, by contrast, more often just means "to leave" or "to go" in everyday speech (我先走了, "I'm heading out now"), a meaning drift away from its ancient sense of brisk walking or running.

components.note: 手 is a simple picture of an open hand with the fingers spread out.
A vertical line 丨 running through the middle of a box or flag 口 — a simple image for the idea of 'center, middle.'

example.hanzi: 主动权掌握在我们手中。
example.pinyin: Zhǔdòngquán zhǎngwò zài wǒmen shǒuzhōng.
example.english: The initiative is in our hands.
example.fact: 手中 joins the concrete 手 ("hand") with 中 ("within, in the middle of") to mean not just "physically in the hand" but, by extension, "within someone's control or possession" — the same literal-to-figurative shift English makes with "in someone's hands."

components.note: 心 (heart/mind) — 想 relates to thinking, missing someone, or wanting something in one's heart.
相 (xiāng) gives the sound — 想 is pronounced xiǎng, matching aside from tone.
冂 (a simplified eye shape in 见's modern form) — emphasizes the act of seeing.
儿 (a person) — a person with an emphasized eye above gives 见 its meaning 'to see.'

example.hanzi: 从他的表情可以想见他有多失望。
example.pinyin: Cóng tā de biǎoqíng kěyǐ xiǎngjiàn tā yǒu duō shīwàng.
example.english: From his expression, one can well imagine how disappointed he is.
example.fact: 想见 isn't "to think about seeing someone," as its parts 想 ("to think") and 见 ("to see") might suggest to a beginner — it actually means "to infer, to vividly imagine," and almost always follows 可以 or 不难 ("可以想见," "不难想见") to introduce a conclusion drawn from indirect evidence.

components.note: 亻 (person) — 伊 originally referred to a person
尹 (yǐn) gives a sound close to 伊's reading yī, sharing a similar historical pronunciation
扌 (hand) — relates directly to 拉's meaning 'to pull, drag,' an action done by hand.
立 (lì) served as the phonetic base; its pronunciation has since drifted noticeably from lā.
十 (here representing a weapon or armor) — 克 pictures overcoming an opponent.
兄 (a person, here representing a formidable figure) — overcoming a strong opponent gave 克 its meaning 'to overcome' or 'to be able to.'

example.hanzi: 那位记者常年在伊拉克报道战争新闻。
example.pinyin: Nà wèi jìzhě chángnián zài Yīlākè bàodào zhànzhēng xīnwén.
example.english: That reporter has reported war news from Iraq for years.
example.fact: 伊拉克 is a sound-only transliteration of "Iraq" — 伊 (a formal third-person pronoun in Classical Chinese), 拉 ("to pull"), and 克 ("gram; to overcome") are chosen purely for their pronunciation, with no attempt at meaning, typical of how Chinese renders country names with no older Chinese-coined equivalent.

components.note: The oracle-bone form has been interpreted as a bird flying up toward the sky; the meaning later shifted entirely to represent negation, 'not.'
止 depicts a footprint, with toes at the top and the leg below — a simple picture of a foot, later extended to mean 'to stop.'

example.hanzi: 这本书我已经看了不止三次。
example.pinyin: Zhè běn shū wǒ yǐjīng kànle bùzhǐ sān cì.
example.english: I've already read this book more than three times.
example.fact: 不止 is easy to confuse with the near-homophone 不只 — 不止 (built on 止, "to stop") literally means "doesn't stop at," giving its sense of "more than, exceeding," while 不只 pairs with 而且 to mean "not only... but also"; mixing up the two characters is a common slip even among native speakers.

components.note: 页 (head) — 顾 originally related to turning the head to look back at something
厄 (è) gives a sound distantly related to 顾's reading gù, having drifted apart over time
口 (mouth) — 问 relates to speaking, specifically asking a question.
门 (mén) gives a hint of the sound — 问 is pronounced wèn, related but the tone and vowel have shifted.

example.hanzi: 他退休后担任公司的顾问。
example.pinyin: Tā tuìxiū hòu dānrèn gōngsī de gùwèn.
example.english: After retiring, he serves as the company's adviser.
example.fact: 顾问 combines 顾 ("to look back at, to consider," from 页 "head" — turning one's head to look) with 问 ("to ask") — literally "one you look to and ask," a fairly transparent image for someone whose job is to be consulted.

components.note: 阝 (mound, related to walls and terrain) — 障 describes something that blocks a path, like a wall.
章 (zhāng) gives a sound close to zhàng, differing only in tone.
石 (stone) — 碍 describes something solid, like a stone, blocking one's path.
㝵 gives a sound closely related to ài, though pronunciation has drifted somewhat over time.

example.hanzi: 语言是他们交流的最大障碍。
example.pinyin: Yǔyán shì tāmen jiāoliú de zuìdà zhàng'ài.
example.english: Language is the biggest obstacle to their communication.
example.fact: Both halves of 障碍 independently mean "to block" — 障 (mound/wall radical 阝) and 碍 (stone radical 石) — a doubled-synonym compound built the same way as 喜欢 and 应该 from the pilot batch, where two near-synonymous characters reinforce a single meaning.

components.note: 厃 depicts a steep, overhanging cliff edge.
㔾 depicts a person crouching — together with 厃, the image of someone perched at a cliff's edge gave 危 its meaning 'dangerous.'
木 (wood) — 机 originally referred to a wooden device or machine, such as a loom.
几 depicts a small table or stool — combined with 木 (wood), the character pictured a wooden machine or mechanism.

example.hanzi: 这家公司正面临严重的财务危机。
example.pinyin: Zhè jiā gōngsī zhèng miànlín yánzhòng de cáiwù wēijī.
example.english: This company is currently facing a serious financial crisis.
example.fact: 危机 combines 危 ("danger," from a pictograph of someone crouched at a cliff's edge) with 机 ("mechanism; pivotal juncture") — the basis for the popular claim that Chinese "crisis" is built from "danger" plus "opportunity." The etymology of the two characters is real, but many linguists caution that 机 here means something closer to "a critical turning point" than "a chance to profit."

components.note: 攵 (to act, strike) — 敏 describes being quick and effective in action, 'nimble, sharp.'
每 (měi) is only distantly related in sound to mǐn — the rhyme has drifted apart over time.
咸 (all, together) — 感 relates to a shared reaction.
心 (heart) — feelings that stir the heart gave 感 its meaning 'to feel' or 'emotion.'

example.hanzi: 这个话题在办公室里很敏感。
example.pinyin: Zhège huàtí zài bàngōngshì lǐ hěn mǐngǎn.
example.english: This topic is very sensitive in the office.
example.fact: 敏感 covers both physical sensitivity (皮肤敏感, "sensitive skin") and social sensitivity (敏感话题, "a sensitive topic"), paralleling English "sensitive" — but 敏 alone already means "quick, sharp-witted," so the word leans toward "quick to perceive or react" rather than "easily hurt."

components.note: 十 (ten) — 博 relates to breadth, with ten symbolizing completeness.
尃 (fū) reflects the character's historical phonetic root, though the modern reading bó has diverged considerably.
牛 (ox/cattle) — cattle were among the earliest and most valuable kinds of property, connecting 物 to the general idea of 'object' or 'thing.'
勿 (wù) gives the sound — 物 is also pronounced wù, an exact match.
饣 (food) points to a place where meals are served.
官 pictures an official hall or residence, giving 馆 its sense of a large public building.

example.hanzi: 周末我们打算去博物馆看展览。
example.pinyin: Zhōumò wǒmen dǎsuàn qù bówùguǎn kàn zhǎnlǎn.
example.english: This weekend we plan to go to the museum to see an exhibition.
example.fact: 博物馆 — literally "hall (馆) of broad (博) things (物)" — is a late-19th/early-20th-century coinage modeled on the Western museum, and is often grouped with words like 经济 and 社会 as one of many modern institutional terms that Chinese picked up via Japanese kanji compounds coined during the Meiji era.

components.note: 冂 depicts a boundary or border enclosing an area.
土 (earth/land) — the land enclosed within the border.
口 here depicts a well within that land — together giving 周 its early meaning of a bounded territory, and later 'circumference, week, the Zhou dynasty.'
五 places an X-shaped cross between two horizontal lines representing heaven and earth — in traditional cosmology, this was linked to the five elements that fill the space between.

example.hanzi: 我们周五晚上有聚会。
example.pinyin: Wǒmen zhōuwǔ wǎnshang yǒu jùhuì.
example.english: We have a get-together on Friday evening.
example.fact: 周五 numbers the weekdays starting from Monday as "one" (周一 Monday ... 周五 Friday), with 周日 or 星期天 set aside for Sunday — a plain numbered system that contrasts with English weekday names rooted in old gods and celestial bodies (Saturn's day, Moon's day, and so on).

components.note: 扌 (hand) — 摄 describes taking hold of or capturing something, as in taking a photograph.
聂 (niè) gives a sound distantly related to shè's reading, having drifted apart over time.
亻 (person) — relates to 像's meaning 'to resemble, be like; image, portrait,' comparing one person or thing to another.
象 (xiàng) gives the sound — 像 is also pronounced xiàng, an exact match.
木 (wood) — 机 originally referred to a wooden device or machine, such as a loom.
几 depicts a small table or stool — combined with 木 (wood), the character pictured a wooden machine or mechanism.

example.hanzi: 婚礼现场架着好几台摄像机。
example.pinyin: Hūnlǐ xiànchǎng jiàzhe hǎojǐ tái shèxiàngjī.
example.english: Several video cameras were set up at the wedding venue.
example.fact: 摄像机 (a video/movie camera) and 照相机 (a still camera) share no character besides the generic 机 ("machine") — 摄 means "to capture, take in" while 照 means "to shine light on, illuminate," a lexical line between capturing motion and capturing a lit still image that English's single word "camera" blurs together.

components.note: 扌 (hand) — 打 relates to hitting or performing an action with the hand.
丁 (dīng) gives the sound — 打 is pronounced dǎ, a connection that has shifted in tone.
石 (rock/stone) — 破 relates to breaking, as a rock can be broken
皮 (pí) gives a loose sound connection to 破's reading pò

example.hanzi: 他打破了世界纪录。
example.pinyin: Tā dǎpòle shìjiè jìlù.
example.english: He broke the world record.
example.fact: Beyond physically shattering an object, 打破 extends metaphorically to breaking records (打破纪录), breaking silence (打破沉默), and breaking old habits or conventions (打破常规) — much like English "break" spans the same range from literal smashing to abstract disruption.

components.note: 手 is a simple picture of an open hand with the fingers spread out.
A short stroke placed below a longer one — the mirror image of 上 (up), together forming a simple, opposite pair.

example.hanzi: 他手下有二十几名员工。
example.pinyin: Tā shǒuxià yǒu èrshí jǐ míng yuángōng.
example.english: He has more than twenty employees under him.
example.fact: 手下 literally means "under the hand" (手 "hand" + 下 "below") and can name one's subordinates (他的手下, "his men") or describe the moment of taking action, as in the idiom 手下留情 — literally "leave mercy under the hand" — meaning "go easy on someone."

components.note: 文 depicts a chest marked with crossing lines, once tattoos or patterns on the body — decoration and pattern gave rise to the idea of 'writing' and 'culture.'

example.hanzi: 每个国家都有自己独特的文化。
example.pinyin: Měi gè guójiā dōu yǒu zìjǐ dútè de wénhuà.
example.english: Every country has its own unique culture.
example.fact: 文化 literally means "the transformation (化) brought about by pattern/writing (文)" — 文 originally pictured decorative markings or tattoos on a chest before broadening to mean "writing, civility, culture." The compound was popularized in its modern sense partly through early-20th-century translations of the Western concept of "culture."

components.note: 马 (simplified from 馬) depicts a horse in profile, with its mane, legs, and tail visible — later simplified into just a few strokes.
十 (here representing a weapon or armor) — 克 pictures overcoming an opponent.
兄 (a person, here representing a formidable figure) — overcoming a strong opponent gave 克 its meaning 'to overcome' or 'to be able to.'

example.hanzi: 马克是我在德国认识的第一个朋友。
example.pinyin: Mǎkè shì wǒ zài Déguó rènshi de dì yī gè péngyou.
example.english: Mark was the first friend I made in Germany.
example.fact: 马克 does double duty as both the transliterated name "Mark" and the old German currency "(Deutsche) Mark" — the same two characters, chosen purely for their sound, happen to cover two unrelated foreign words, a common outcome when Chinese borrows short foreign terms phonetically.

components.note: 辶 (to walk) suggests following a path.
尊 (to honor) shows respect for what is being followed, giving 遵 its meaning 'to obey, to comply with.'
宀 (walls/roof) — the boundary of a home to be protected
寸 (a hand) — keeping watch, holding the space within the walls

example.hanzi: 每个员工都应该遵守公司的规定。
example.pinyin: Měi gè yuángōng dōu yīnggāi zūnshǒu gōngsī de guīdìng.
example.english: Every employee should abide by the company's rules.
example.fact: 遵守 pairs 遵 ("to follow respectfully," 辶 "to walk" + 尊 "to honor") with 守 ("to guard, keep to") for the everyday word for obeying rules or laws; its more formal cousin 遵循 swaps in 循 ("to follow a path") for a slightly more written, bookish register.

components.note: A simplified pictograph of a bird's wings spread in flight — the source of 飞's meaning 'to fly.'
舟 (boat) — 船 is a vessel that travels on water, directly tied to its meaning 'ship, boat'

example.hanzi: 神舟飞船成功返回地球。
example.pinyin: Shénzhōu fēichuán chénggōng fǎnhuí dìqiú.
example.english: The Shenzhou spacecraft successfully returned to Earth.
example.fact: 飞船 literally means "flying boat" (飞 "to fly" + 船 "boat, ship") — the same nautical metaphor that English reaches for in "spaceship," both languages independently borrowing a seafaring vessel to describe travel through a vast, uncharted medium.

components.note: 亻 (person) — 保 relates to a person looking after or protecting someone, originally a caretaker holding a child.
呆 (dāi) gives a hint of the sound — 保 is pronounced bǎo, a connection that has shifted over time.
宀 (walls/roof) — the boundary of a home to be protected
寸 (a hand) — keeping watch, holding the space within the walls

example.hanzi: 他的政治观点比较保守。
example.pinyin: Tā de zhèngzhì guāndiǎn bǐjiào bǎoshǒu.
example.english: His political views are relatively conservative.
example.fact: 保守 works as a verb ("to guard, preserve," 保守秘密 "to keep a secret") and as an adjective ("conservative," 保守派 "conservatives") — the verb sense of protecting something as it is came first, and the adjective sense of resisting change grew out of it, a semantic drift English's own word "conservative" also went through.

components.note: 纟 (thread/silk) — 维 relates to a connecting thread or fiber, extended to mean 'to maintain, to link'
隹 (zhuī) gives a loose sound connection to 维's reading wéi
扌 (hand) — relates directly to 持's meaning 'to hold, maintain.'
寺 (sì) served as the phonetic base; its pronunciation has since drifted well away from chí.

example.hanzi: 这个国家一直努力维持和平。
example.pinyin: Zhège guójiā yìzhí nǔlì wéichí hépíng.
example.english: This country has always worked hard to maintain peace.
example.fact: 维持 combines 维 ("a connecting thread or fiber," silk radical 纟) with 持 ("to hold," hand radical 扌) — a thread held taut is the image behind 维持's core sense of keeping something from slackening or falling apart, whether it's peace, order, or a relationship.

components.note: 丶 (a dot) — represents the burning flame atop a lamp.
王 here depicts the base and stand of an oil lamp, not its usual meaning 'king' — the one who tends the flame became linked to 'master, lord, main.'
⺮ (bamboo) — 管 originally referred to a bamboo pipe or tube, later broadening to mean 'to manage' or 'to control.'
官 (guān) gives a hint of the sound — 管 is pronounced guǎn, a connection that has shifted only slightly in tone.

example.hanzi: 这件事由市场部主管负责。
example.pinyin: Zhè jiàn shì yóu shìchǎngbù zhǔguǎn fùzé.
example.english: This matter is handled by the marketing department manager.
example.fact: 主管 works as both a noun ("the person in charge, a supervisor") and a verb ("to be in charge of," 主管财务 "to be in charge of finances") — the same flexible pattern as English "head" ("the department head" vs. "to head the department").

components.note: 丶 (a dot) — represents the burning flame atop a lamp.
王 here depicts the base and stand of an oil lamp, not its usual meaning 'king' — the one who tends the flame became linked to 'master, lord, main.'
⺷ (sheep, related to 羊) — 义 relates to what is right or moral, linked to the idea of sacrificial sheep used in rituals of righteousness.
乂 (yì) gives the sound — 义 is also pronounced yì, an exact match.

example.hanzi: 他是一个理想主义者。
example.pinyin: Tā shì yí gè lǐxiǎng zhǔyìzhě.
example.english: He is an idealist.
example.fact: 主义 is Chinese's standard suffix for translating the Western "-ism" (社会主义 "socialism," 现实主义 "realism"), literally "guiding principle" from 主 ("master, lord") + 义 ("righteousness, doctrine") — one of the most productive loan-translation patterns in modern Chinese, coined largely through 19th/20th-century contact with Japanese kanji compounds.

components.note: 巾 (cloth) — 常 originally referred to a long skirt or banner made of cloth, later coming to mean something 'usual' or 'ordinary.'
尚 (shàng) gives a hint of the sound — 常 is pronounced cháng, a connection that has drifted over time.
巾 (cloth) — 常 originally referred to a long skirt or banner made of cloth, later coming to mean something 'usual' or 'ordinary.'
尚 (shàng) gives a hint of the sound — 常 is pronounced cháng, a connection that has drifted over time.

example.hanzi: 我们常常一起去公园散步。
example.pinyin: Wǒmen chángcháng yìqǐ qù gōngyuán sànbù.
example.english: We often go to the park together to take walks.
example.fact: 常常 is simply 常 ("usual, often") reduplicated, functioning as an adverb of frequency close to 经常 — but unlike 经常, which can occasionally modify a noun in formal contexts, 常常 sits almost exclusively right before a verb, a subtle difference between two very close synonyms.

components.note: 扌 (hand) — 摄 describes taking hold of or capturing something, as in taking a photograph.
聂 (niè) gives a sound distantly related to shè's reading, having drifted apart over time.
彡 (fine lines) — suggests light and shadow, relating to 影's meaning 'shadow, image.'
景 (jǐng) gives a sound hint — 影 is pronounced yǐng, sharing the same rhyme though the initial consonant differs.
帀 (a banner or covering) — flying above the scene.
刂 (a knife) — wielded with skill beneath the banner, an image of expertise giving 师 its meaning 'master, teacher, expert.'

example.hanzi: 这位摄影师拍的婚纱照非常漂亮。
example.pinyin: Zhè wèi shèyǐngshī pāi de hūnshā zhào fēicháng piàoliang.
example.english: The wedding photos this photographer took are very beautiful.
example.fact: 摄影师 stacks three meaningful pieces — 摄 ("to capture"), 影 ("shadow, image," built on 彡 "fine lines" for light and shadow), and the suffix 师 ("master, skilled professional") — literally "a master of capturing images," the same 师 that turns 工程 into "engineer" or plain 老 into "teacher."

components.note: 土 (earth/soil) — 地's original meaning is 'earth, ground'
也 (yě) gives a partial sound match for 地's other reading dì; in this grammatical-particle usage the character is instead pronounced 'de'

example.hanzi: 我们在山脚下的营地过了一夜。
example.pinyin: Wǒmen zài shānjiǎo xià de yíngdì guòle yí yè.
example.english: We spent a night at the campsite at the foot of the mountain.
example.fact: 营 originally referred to a military camp or barracks — where troops were quartered — and 营地 only broadened beyond that strictly military root to cover recreational or refugee camps (夏令营 "summer camp," 难民营 "refugee camp") in more modern usage.

components.note: 承 depicts multiple hands supporting and lifting something from below — giving 承 its meaning 'to support, to receive, to inherit.'
扌 (hand) — 担 relates to carrying something, often on a shoulder pole
旦 (dàn) gives a sound close to 担's reading dān, sharing a similar historical pronunciation

example.hanzi: 公司必须承担这次事故的责任。
example.pinyin: Gōngsī bìxū chéngdān zhè cì shìgù de zérèn.
example.english: The company must bear responsibility for this accident.
example.fact: 承 alone pictures multiple hands lifting something from below, and 担 (hand radical 扌 + phonetic 旦) relates to carrying a load, often on a shoulder pole — 承担 layers two separate "carrying" images into one verb for taking on a duty or responsibility.

components.note: 扌 (hand) — 指 relates to using the hand, specifically the fingers.
旨 (an aim, purpose) — combined with 扌 (hand), 指 came to mean 'finger' and 'to point,' aiming the hand at something.
军 (army) — an army being directed
扌 (hand) — the hand giving the command or wave

example.hanzi: 指挥官下令全体撤退。
example.pinyin: Zhǐhuīguān xiàlìng quántǐ chètuì.
example.english: The commander ordered a full retreat.
example.fact: 指挥官 adds the suffix 官 ("officer, official") onto 指挥 ("to direct, command," literally 指 "to point" + 挥 "to wave," the gestures of someone directing troops) — 指挥 alone already stands as a verb for "to conduct/direct," including conducting an orchestra (指挥乐队), while 官 narrows it specifically to a military commander.

components.note: A drawing of a person standing with arms and legs spread wide — used to represent the idea of something being 'big' or 'great.'
广 (a building/shelter) — 厅 names a large room inside a building, a hall.
丁 (dīng) gives a sound close to tīng.

example.hanzi: 酒店大厅装饰得很豪华。
example.pinyin: Jiǔdiàn dàtīng zhuāngshì de hěn háohuá.
example.english: The hotel lobby is decorated very luxuriously.
example.fact: 厅 (building radical 广 + phonetic 丁) already means "a large room, hall" by itself — 大厅 simply reinforces that with 大 ("big"), producing a grander, more emphatic word for a hall or lobby, similar to how English sometimes says "great hall" for emphasis rather than just "hall."

components.note: 屮 (a young sprout) growing up and out of 凵 (a container or pit) — a picture of something emerging, hence 'going out.'

example.hanzi: 那条路经常出事,大家开车要小心。
example.pinyin: Nà tiáo lù jīngcháng chūshì, dàjiā kāichē yào xiǎoxīn.
example.english: Accidents often happen on that road, so everyone should drive carefully.
example.fact: 出事 is a verb-object compound (出 "to emerge, happen" + 事 "matter, incident") that's already grammatically complete, so it can't take a further direct object — "to have a car accident" needs the separate phrase 出车祸 rather than stacking a new object onto 出事.

components.note: 扌 (hand) — 打 relates to hitting or performing an action with the hand.
丁 (dīng) gives the sound — 打 is pronounced dǎ, a connection that has shifted in tone.
扌 (hand) — 扫 describes using the hand to sweep.
帚 depicts a hand-held broom — held by the hand 扌, it gave 扫 its meaning 'to sweep.'

example.hanzi: 周末我们一起打扫房间。
example.pinyin: Zhōumò wǒmen yìqǐ dǎsǎo fángjiān.
example.english: On the weekend we clean the room together.
example.fact: 打扫 pairs 打 — a nearly meaningless "light verb" that shows up in many compound verbs, like 打电话 ("to phone") or 打篮球 ("to play basketball") — with 扫 ("to sweep," hand radical 扌 + 帚, a picture of a hand-held broom); 打 here contributes little beyond turning 扫 into a smoother two-syllable verb.
